notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Zechariah 8, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## ZECHARIAH 8 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### Overview / Structure

The chapter is the second half of the LORD's answer to the question about fasting posed in Zechariah 7. It divides into two main sections (vv. 1–17 and vv. 18–23), each introduced by "the word of the LORD of hosts came to me." The tenfold repetition of "Thus saith the LORD of hosts" (vv. 2, 3, 4–5, 6, 7, 9, 14, 19, 20, 23) underscores that these are divine revelations, not human words. Some commentators call this "a decalogue of divine words." The name "LORD of hosts" appears 18 times in this chapter alone, emphasising that what is promised is impossible for man but must be accomplished by the Almighty.

— Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); NET Bible notes (via https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23); Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries)

---

### v. 1 — "Again the word of the LORD of Hosts came to me, saying:"

After the solemn warnings that closed chapter 7, this verse marks a transition to comfort and encouragement. Gill notes that the Hebrew lacks "to me" here (the only place in Zechariah where it is missing in the Hebrew, though the Targum supplies "with me"). The Pulpit Commentary observes that when warning is carried too far it degenerates into threatening and produces despair; thus the chapter turns to an animating series of encouragements.

— Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html)

---

### v. 2 — "I am jealous for Zion with great zeal; I am jealous for her with great fervor."

The Hebrew word translated "zealous" / "jealous" comes from a root meaning "to become intensely red," picturing a face flushed with deep emotion. God is passionately concerned for His people. Ellicott notes the verb should read "I am" (present), not "I was" — God declares His ongoing, burning love for Zion. The Pulpit Commentary explains that the "great fury" (or "fervor") is directed *against her enemies*: God's jealousy has two sides — light and protection for Israel, darkness and destruction for her foes, like the pillar of fire in Exodus 14:20. Gill connects this to Zechariah 1:14 and sees a double reference — literal Jerusalem and the Church in Gospel times; the "fury" is against Babylonians then and antichristian powers later.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem. Then Jerusalem will be called the City of Truth, and the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain."

God promises His personal return and dwelling in Jerusalem. When God departed, the city fell; His return transforms it. "City of Truth" (or "faithful city," cf. Isaiah 1:26) means a place where truth and fidelity toward God have their home, no longer full of lies and treachery. "Holy Mountain" refers to the temple mount sanctified by God's presence. Gill sees this fulfilled in Christ's incarnation — "the Word was made flesh and dwelt (tabernacled) among us" — and ultimately in the New Jerusalem where "nothing that makes a lie" shall enter (Rev 21:27). The Pulpit Commentary says this received a partial fulfilment between Zerubbabel and Christ but awaits a further, complete accomplishment. Guzik applies it spiritually: when God's presence is real in our lives, we become people of truth and holiness.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### vv. 4–5 — "Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem, each with a staff in hand because of great age. And the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there."

A picture of happy security, long life, and peace, in vivid contrast to the desolation described in Lamentations. In Zechariah's day Jerusalem's walls were ruined and the city was unsafe for the most vulnerable. Ellicott notes this was fulfilled to the letter in the days of Simon the Maccabee (1 Maccabees 14:4–15), when "the ancient men sat in all the streets…and there was none to fray them." The Pulpit Commentary adds that length of days was the reward of obedience under the old covenant (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 4:40). The Church Pulpit Commentary remarks that "little children and old people are the greatest blessings of a nation, and the surest test of its government." Guzik notes the absence of elderly people in the struggling returned community made this promise especially poignant; he also cites J. Vernon McGee's quip that this verse suggests there will be no cars in millennial Jerusalem.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Church Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/zechariah-8.html)

---

### v. 6 — "If this is impossible in the eyes of the remnant of this people in these days, should it also be impossible in My eyes?"

The promise of a transformed, prosperous, safe Jerusalem seemed incredible to the struggling returned exiles (the walls wouldn't be rebuilt for another 60 years). Ellicott renders the Hebrew better as: "Though it was marvellous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, will it therefore be marvellous in mine eyes?" The point echoes Genesis 18:14 and Matthew 19:26 — "with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Guzik quotes Spurgeon at length: a boy visiting a nobleman's house was amazed at its grandeur, only to be told "this is only the kitchen!" — so we have seen only the kitchen of God's great house, not yet the palace. Gill notes some take this not as a question but as an affirmation: God would indeed do that which was marvellous.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### vv. 7–8 — "I will save My people from the land of the east and from the land of the west. I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem, where they will be My people, and I will be their faithful and righteous God."

Proportionately few exiles had returned under Zerubbabel. God now promises a far greater gathering — not only from Babylon (the east) but from the west also, symbolising the whole world (Psalm 50:1; Malachi 1:11). Ellicott notes there were indeed Jews in exile in the west (Joel 3:6; Isaiah 43:5–6). The gathering is not merely geographic but spiritual: "They shall be My people and I will be their God, in truth and righteousness." This is covenant renewal language. The Pulpit Commentary stresses that "in truth and in righteousness" applies to both sides: God will deal truly with them, but they must also deal truly with Him. The NET Bible notes mark this as "a restoration of the unbroken fellowship" that Israel's disloyalty had shattered, ultimately fulfilled in the eschaton (cf. Jeremiah 31:33).

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)

---

### vv. 9–10 — "Let your hands be strong, you who now hear these words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid to rebuild the temple … For before those days neither man nor beast received wages, nor was there safety from the enemy … for I had turned every man against his neighbor."

"Let your hands be strong" is an encouragement to press on with rebuilding the temple. The foundation had been laid more than 15 years earlier, but work had stalled. Ellicott suggests there may have been other prophets besides Haggai and Zechariah who spoke at that time, and that "that the temple might be built" refers to the *resumption* of building (c. 520 BC), not the initial foundation-laying in 536 BC (Ezra 3:10) which was followed by 16 years of inactivity. Verse 10 recalls the hardship before the work resumed: no wages, no safety, internal strife. The Pulpit Commentary explains that the march of Cambyses' Persian army south through Palestine added to the people's distress. Gill notes the lack of hire for man or beast "turned to any account" — wages earned were as if put into a bag with holes (cf. Haggai 1:6).

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### vv. 11–12 — "But now I will not treat the remnant of this people as I did in the past … For the seed will be prosperous, the vine will yield its fruit, the ground will yield its produce, and the skies will give their dew."

God announces a change in His dealings: the curse is being lifted. "The seed shall be prosperous" is literally "the seed of peace" in Hebrew. The Pulpit Commentary discusses various interpretations: (a) crops will be safe and secure rather than devoured by enemies (cf. Leviticus 26:16); (b) the phrase is in apposition to "the vine" (i.e., "the seed of peace, the vine"), though this rendering is criticised because vines were propagated from cuttings, not seed; (c) peace will be radically established and from that agricultural blessing flows. Gill connects this directly to Haggai's prophecies (Haggai 1:6, 10–11; 2:19) where drought and blight are reversed once the people prioritise the temple. The "remnant" who will "possess all these things" are those who, seeking first spiritual things, have material blessings added (cf. Matthew 6:33).

— Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/)

---

### v. 13 — "As you have been a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you will be a blessing. Do not be afraid; let your hands be strong."

Israel's fate had become a formula of imprecation among the nations — "May your fate be that of the Jews" (cf. Jeremiah 24:9; 29:22). God now promises the reverse: they will become a formula of blessing (cf. Genesis 48:20; Ruth 4:11–12). The address to both "house of Judah and house of Israel" indicates all twelve tribes, reunited after the exile. Spurgeon preached on this verse, noting four truths: (1) the unconverted are a curse, (2) when converted they become a blessing, (3) the transformation is wrought by God ("I will save you"), (4) encouragement follows: "Fear not, but let your hands be strong." Spurgeon applied this to the individual believer: every unconverted person "adds another handful of leaven to leaven the whole lump," but those whom God saves become a positive blessing to the world.

— Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/zechariah-8.html and https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/once-a-curse-but-now-a-blessing); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### vv. 14–15 — "Just as I resolved to bring disaster upon you when your fathers provoked Me to anger, and I did not relent … so now I have resolved to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah. Do not be afraid."

God's past faithfulness in judgment is the guarantee of His future faithfulness in blessing. Just as He "repented not" (did not relent) concerning the decreed punishment, so now His determination to do good is equally firm. The Pulpit Commentary calls this the "ground of the promise": the will of God, who cannot deceive. Guzik quotes Unger: "God's strange work is judgment. His delight is to bless His people." The past chastisement stands as proof that when God purposes something, it happens — both for evil and for good (Isaiah 14:24).

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

---

### vv. 16–17 — "These are the things you must do: Speak truth to one another, render true and sound judgments in your gates, do not plot evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and do not love to swear falsely, for I hate all these things."

The promised blessings are conditional on obedience. Four ethical commands correspond to the character of the "City of Truth": (1) speak truth — quoted by Paul in Ephesians 4:25; (2) render true judgments that promote peace (cf. Zechariah 7:9); (3) do not plot evil in the heart — hatred without a cause was, according to Jarchi, the cause of the destruction of the second temple; (4) do not love false oaths. Gill notes that the prevalent sins in the post-exilic period were not idolatry but commercial dishonesty — cheating, lying, and injustice learned in Babylon. "Your gates" refers to the place where judges sat and justice was administered (Deuteronomy 16:18). God's hatred of these things is given as the ultimate reason to avoid them.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html)

---

### vv. 18–19 — "The fasts of the fourth, the fifth, the seventh, and the tenth months will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah. Therefore you are to love both truth and peace."

This is the direct answer to the delegation's original question in Zechariah 7:3. The four fasts commemorated tragedies in the fall of Jerusalem:
- **Fourth month (Tammuz):** the breaching of the city walls (Jeremiah 39:2; also the 17th of Tammuz commemorated the breaking of the tablets of the Law).
- **Fifth month (Ab):** the burning of the temple (Jeremiah 52:12–13).
- **Seventh month (Tishri):** the murder of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25; also the Day of Atonement on the 10th).
- **Tenth month (Tebeth):** the beginning of the siege (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4).

God does not command the abolition of these fasts but promises such blessing that they will be transformed into "joy and gladness and cheerful feasts." G. Campbell Morgan (quoted in Guzik) said: "None of these things had been in the purpose of God for His people; they had resulted from their sins. The fasts therefore were the result of their sins." According to Jewish tradition (T.B. Rosh Hashanah 18b), when the nation was in peace the fasts were held in abeyance; when in trouble, they were resumed. Maimonides stated that all these fasts shall cease in the days of the Messiah. The command to "love truth and peace" echoes the ethical conditions of vv. 16–17.

— Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)

---

### vv. 20–22 — "Peoples will yet come — the residents of many cities — and the residents of one city will go to another, saying: 'Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts. I myself am going.' And many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Hosts in Jerusalem and to plead before the LORD."

The language echoes Micah 4:2 and Isaiah 2:2–3. In Zechariah's day, few wanted to come to a ruined city. God now promises that the nations will stream to Jerusalem to seek the LORD. Ellicott says "we must not look for a literal fulfilment" — the prophecy is "virtually fulfilled in the fact that through Jesus Christ (who was a Jew according to the flesh) the knowledge of the true God has been spread among most nations of the world," though "in view of Romans 11, we are not without warrant in looking forward to a more glorious and perfect fulfilment." The Pulpit Commentary likewise says the literal fulfilment is not to be looked for; it declares "the future conversion of the Gentiles, and their being made one with Israel in the Church of Christ, 'one fold under one Shepherd' (John 10:16)." The NET Bible notes see an initial fulfilment in the establishment of the church (Acts 2:5–11) and ultimate completion in the messianic age (Isaiah 45:14, 24; Zechariah 14:16–21). Guzik takes a more futurist view: this will be fulfilled literally in the millennial kingdom when Jerusalem is the headquarters of Christ's reign.

— Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/)

---

### v. 23 — "In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue will tightly grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'"

"Ten" is an indefinite number for a large multitude (Genesis 31:7; cf. "seven" in Isaiah 4:1). The Hebrew word for "grasp" (ḥāzaq) is the same verb used for grabbing a snake by the tail (Exodus 4:4) or a lion by its beard (1 Samuel 17:35) — a grip that will not let go. The Pulpit Commentary pictures a Jew journeying to Jerusalem for a festival, with Gentiles clinging to him asking to come along because they have heard that God is with His people. Gill sees this as a prophecy of the "calling and conversion of the Gentiles" joining with Jewish believers. Ellicott says the prophecy is fulfilled through Christ — "that one Jew, Jesus of Nazareth" (Boice, quoted by Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary adds that "the true Israelites are not merely those who are of the natural posterity of Abraham, but all true Christians united under Christ, the Head" (cf. Romans 4:11; Galatians 3:7, 29). St. Jerome discerned the Messiah in "the man that is a Jew." Precept Austin calls this "one of the most remarkable statements in all of Scripture" — a time when Israel is no longer despised but sought after because God's presence is manifestly with them.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm); Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)

---

## WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS DIFFER

### Eschatology: Is the fulfilment literal (millennial) or spiritual (church age)?

The key disagreement among Protestant traditions on Zechariah 8 concerns whether its promises will be fulfilled **literally in a future millennium** or **spiritually in the present church age** (or both).

- **Dispensational / Futurist (common among many Baptists, Pentecostals, and some Reformed):** David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal tradition) reads the chapter as pointing to a literal future millennial kingdom. The gathering from east and west (vv. 7–8), the nations streaming to Jerusalem (vv. 20–23), and the safety of the city (vv. 4–5) all await fulfilment when Christ reigns from Jerusalem. The NET Bible notes likewise call vv. 4–5 "eschatological in tone" and reference the millennial kingdom (Isaiah 65:20; Jeremiah 31:12–13). Dr. Constable (cited in search results, Dallas Theological Seminary) states: "The whole chapter presents Israel's eventual restoration and participation in full millennial blessing." The Precept Austin overview says plainly: "Jerusalem will be the world capital (Isaiah 2:1–5)" and "Jerusalem will become the religious capital as well as the center of God's government."

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-8.html); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)

- **Covenant / Amillennial / Postmillennial (common in historic Reformed, Lutheran, and some Anglican readings):** Ellicott (Anglican bishop and scholar, 1878) explicitly states that the gathering of nations to Jerusalem in vv. 20–23 "we must not look for a literal fulfilment." It is "virtually fulfilled, in the fact that through Jesus Christ (who was a Jew according to the flesh) the knowledge of the true God has been spread among most nations of the world." The Pulpit Commentary (broadly evangelical, 1880) agrees: "The literal fulfilment of this prophecy is not to be looked for. It declares the future conversion of the Gentiles, and their being made one with Israel in the Church of Christ." However, Ellicott also allows that "in view of Romans 11, we are not without warrant in looking forward to a more glorious and perfect fulfilment of such prophecies as this in the unknown future" — a hint toward a future for ethnic Israel without adopting full dispensationalism.

— Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-8.html); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html)

- **Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist):** Spurgeon preached from v. 13 in a way that emphasised individual conversion — the unconverted are a curse, the converted a blessing — applying the text broadly. On v. 19, he acknowledged that "this prophecy may relate to the Jews, literally, and it is referred to by their learned doctors as to the days of the Messiah" and "we look for it to be fulfilled in the latter days," but he also applied it spiritually to the church: "when God returns to bless His Church there are certain signs and marks of His return."

— Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/zechariah-8.html; https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/once-a-curse-but-now-a-blessing)

### The "Seed of Peace" (v. 12)

There is significant divergence on the Hebrew phrase "the seed of peace" (זֶרַע הַשָּׁלוֹם). The Pulpit Commentary surveys several views and rejects the interpretation that "the seed of peace" is in apposition to "the vine" (i.e., "the seed of peace — the vine — shall give its fruit"), noting that vines were propagated by cuttings, not seed, and there is no special reason to call the vine "seed of peace." The Pulpit prefers "crops of peace" — farming labours that succeed in security. Others (Alexander, cited in Pulpit) take "seed of peace" to mean peace will be radically established and agricultural blessing flows from that. The Syriac reads simply "the seed shall be safe."

— Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html)

### The Conditionality of the Promises

Guzik (from a Pentecostal/charismatic perspective) frames vv. 16–17 in terms of the Mosaic covenant: "If God will bless instead of curse, they must fulfill their end of the Mosaic covenant." The Pulpit Commentary likewise presents the blessings as "conditional on their obedience." This reflects a broadly Protestant reading that sees these ethical commands as the human response required for the reception of divine blessing. The NET Bible's emphasis on the name "LORD of hosts" appearing 18 times in the chapter highlights a complementary truth: "the sheer human impossibility of accomplishing what lies ahead — it must be done by the Lord who rules over all," reflecting a Reformed emphasis on divine sovereignty even alongside human responsibility.

— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-8/); Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)

---

## OTHER VIEWS

### Older Commentators on the Fulfilment in Christ

- **Gill (Baptist, 18th century):** Throughout his commentary, Gill applies the chapter spiritually to the Gospel church. "I will save my people from the east country and from the west country" refers not to a literal regathering but to the apostolic mission — the disciples went forth east, west, north, and south to save the Lord's people, both Jews and Gentiles (Malachi 1:11). The "city of truth" is fulfilled when Christ, who is Truth itself, was in Jerusalem, and the Gospel was preached there. The nations grasping the Jew's robe represents Gentile converts joining Jewish believers in the church.

— Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/8.htm)

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran, 19th century):** In their overview (captured in search results), they describe the chapter as "Renewal and Completion of the Covenant of Grace," containing a double promise to Israel on "the simple condition of their observing the moral precepts of the law." The fast-day answer in v. 19 is prefaced by the condition in vv. 16–17: "only when the condition … has been fulfilled."

— Keil & Delitzsch (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/zechariah/8.htm)

### Catholic Reading (via Jerome)

- The Pulpit Commentary reports that **St. Jerome** discerned the Messiah in "the man that is a Jew" of v. 23. St. Cyril of Alexandria saw the Gentiles clinging to Jews "like children holding their fathers' dress for support and guidance." The broader Catholic tradition reads this chapter as a prophecy of the Church — the New Jerusalem — into which the Gentiles are gathered through Christ.

— Pulpit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-8.html)

### NET Bible Notes (Modern Evangelical Scholarship)

The NET Bible translation notes provide several distinctive contributions:
- **v. 3:** The name "truthful city," "mountain of the LORD," and "holy mountain" are seen as eschatological titles for the restored Jerusalem.
- **v. 9:** The "founding" refers to the resumption of work in 520 BC, not the initial 536 BC foundation.
- **v. 14:** The Hebrew verb זָמַם (*zamam*) usually means "to plot to do evil," but with a divine subject and in light of v. 15's plan for good, it means the "implementation of discipline" — God may bring hurt but its purpose is redemptive.
- **v. 23:** The scene finds "initial fulfillment in the establishment of the church (Acts 2:5–11) but ultimate completion in the messianic age (Isa 45:14, 24; 60:14; Zech 14:16–21)."

— NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=zec+8%3A1-23)
